The straight-line solutions of the system have the form

$$
{c}_{1}{e}^{{\lambda }_{1}t}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 3\end{aligned}]\,\text{and}\,{c}_{2}{e}^{{\lambda }_{2}t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

The line that passes through the origin and is parallel to ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 3\end{aligned}]$ has the equation 

$$
y=-3x,
$$

as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14072827/assets/ed058963b391a4cdc66b2ab48483906a4d07759681c1f24e47ffc9e10775895f.png)

${c}_{1}{e}^{{\lambda }_{1}t}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 3\end{aligned}]$
must approach $\text{the origin}$ as $t\to \infty .$ So, we must have ${\lambda }_{1}<0.$

The line that passes through the origin and is parallel to ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$ has the equation 

$$
y=x,
$$

as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14072827/assets/6c92028370c86431ddc6ccd9513c273054d98b5add159e1bddf5a2e11751d987.png)

${c}_{2}{e}^{{\lambda }_{2}t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$
must approach $\text{infinity}$ as $t\to \infty .$ So, we must have ${\lambda }_{2}>0.$

questions.worked_solution:
The general solution of the system is

$$
[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]={c}_{1}{e}^{4t}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}{e}^{3t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.
$$

The line that passes through the origin and is parallel to ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1\end{aligned}]$ has the equation 

$$
y=-\frac{1}{2}x
$$

and the straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{1}{e}^{4t}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1\end{aligned}]$
lie on that line. 

Since ${e}^{4t}\to \infty $ as $t\to \infty ,$ these solutions approach $\text{infinity}$ as $t\to \infty .$

Let's add the solutions to the phase space.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14072827/assets/1d2a232b4351c84871d89ba25384aa53777760355ceea6458b07fba9c0a9ed78.png)

The line that passes through the origin and is parallel to ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$ has the equation 

$$
y=0
$$

and the straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{2}{e}^{3t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$
lie on that line.

Since ${e}^{3t}\to \infty $ as $t\to \infty ,$ these solutions approach $\text{infinity}$ as $t\to \infty .$

Let's add the solutions to the phase space.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14072827/assets/122759a459c8dd56dbe69c44c0da4ccffbbc660465fbedc7457e17b42430436e.png)

For this particular system, we have

$$
0<{\lambda }_{2}<{\lambda }_{1}
$$

thus, ${\lambda }_{1}=4$ is the dominant eigenvalue.

Since the dominant eigenvalue is ${\lambda }_{1}=4,$  solutions become parallel to the straight-line solution containing the vector  ${v}_{1}$ as they move away from the origin.

$$
{c}_{1}{e}^{{\lambda }_{1}t}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\,\text{and}\,{c}_{2}{e}^{{\lambda }_{2}t}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

The line that passes through the origin and is parallel to ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$ has the equation 

$$
y=\frac{1}{2}x,
$$

as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14072827/assets/97f7eb1fbddcd9d927447978efd4c42e705d6835bf0cc74525d42ded8c35346b.png)

The tangents along this line are pointing $\text{away from the origin},$ meaning that the solutions of the form 
${c}_{1}{e}^{{\lambda }_{1}t}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$
must approach $\text{infinity}$ as $t\to \infty .$ So, we must have ${\lambda }_{1}>0.$

The line that passes through the origin and is parallel to ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$ has the equation 

$$
y=-x,
$$

as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14072827/assets/edc697ab38ae9a56d46181e0a45982b7045224de0cc3c4a786ddbc515f22196c.png)

${c}_{2}{e}^{{\lambda }_{2}t}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$
must approach $\text{infinity}$ as $t\to \infty .$ So, we must have ${\lambda }_{2}>0.$

So, for this particular system, both eigenvalues are positive. The dominant eigenvalue is the one with the greatest magnitude.

Now, since the solutions become parallel to the straight-line solution containing the vector ${v}_{1}$ as they move away from the origin, the dominant eigenvalue is ${\lambda }_{1}.$

Therefore, ${\lambda }_{1}>{\lambda }_{2}>0.$
